summary: Live bench of what happens to a command that does NOT succeed (tools/fleetbench/bench_iotsan_commands.py). myiotsan argues hard for one design decision - an actuation is never automatically retried, because re-sending a relay write is a second physical action and a retry whose first attempt landed opens the door twice - and that promise has two halves. Nothing retries is the easy half. Nothing is silently lost is the half that makes the first one safe: refusing to retry is only defensible because a HUMAN is handed the decision, so a command that reaches no human is a silent drop rather than a safe refusal, and a command left neither confirmed nor failed is worse than a retry because nobody is told, nothing counts it, and the row claims to be in flight forever. The bench found two ways a command was lost, and fixed both. ONE REPORT CONFIRMED THREE COMMANDS. Confirmation matched a device's report against its outstanding commands by comparing the reported NUMBER alone, ignoring which telemetry key the report arrived on. A building controller routinely has several commands outstanding that share a number - a lock and a fan are both switches, so both are 1 - so reporting the lock's state marked the fan `confirmed`, which is the strongest claim this system makes about a physical action, and the fan's command then never became the failure the operator would have been shown. One report invented an actuation and lost a failure in the same stroke. It also confirmed a command whose profile declares NO confirm key, the case the code itself documents as an honest "sent, never confirmed" (a bulb that reports colour per-channel cannot be confirmed against one packed float). Confirmation now requires the report to be on the key the profile declares as that command's ConfirmKey, a command declaring none is never confirmed by telemetry at all, and a device whose profile cannot be read confirms nothing - a timeout and an honest "not confirmed" costs less than a false claim that a relay moved. The matching rule is a pure function (confirmsKey) pinned by a unit test. A COMMAND INTERRUPTED MID-WRITE STAYED PENDING FOREVER. The row is written down BEFORE the send, deliberately and correctly - an actuation that was sent but never recorded is the worst possible ordering - but SweepUnconfirmed only ever looked at rows in `sent`, so a process that stopped in between left a row no timeout applied to: never swept, never counted, never notified, and rendered by the UI as still in flight, a spinner that never resolves. The sweep now ends stale `pending` rows too, timed from RequestedAt because such a row has no SentAt (that being exactly what it never got), with a reason that distinguishes the two cases honestly: an unconfirmed command was definitely sent, an interrupted one may never have left the building. The cutoff is the existing 30s confirm window, comfortably longer than any legitimate stay in pending (the MQTT publish is in-process and the Modbus write is bounded by modbusWriteTimeout). Everything else about the lifecycle held, and is now proven rather than assumed: an unconfirmed command becomes failed on the timeout and NOTHING is re-sent across the whole window; the failure reaches the operator's notification feed; a late report does not resurrect a failed command; the twin still shows the disagreement; a restart with a command in flight ends that command and re-sends nothing; and a wedged Modbus device is dialled exactly once per attempt with no re-dial after a restart. The bench drives the hard cases for real: a socket that accepts and never answers stalls a Modbus write inside its per-operation timeout (the window a docker kill has to land in) and counts dials, which is how "nothing re-drove it" is measured on the polled transport; the device that CONFIRMS is the same real MQTT client that watches the wire, so a confirmation is the product's own loop closing rather than an API poke. 34/34 against the fixes; the identical bench file scores 27/32 against unfixed main (two of the 34 checks - the interruption's reason text and its notification - are only reachable once an interrupted command actually ends).
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no API, schema or configuration change. Two behaviours change, both narrowing a claim the product already documents. A device report now confirms only the commands whose profile declares that telemetry key as their ConfirmKey: a command that used to be confirmed by an unrelated key's report of the same value now stays `sent` and ends as an honest `failed` on the confirm timeout, which is the outcome the entity and the technical spec already described. A command declaring no ConfirmKey can no longer be confirmed by telemetry at all - it reaches `sent` and then `failed`, the documented "sent is the best that can ever be said". And a command left `pending` by a process that stopped mid-send is now ended as `failed` after the 30s confirm window instead of remaining `pending` indefinitely; nothing is re-sent in either case. Modbus commands are unaffected by the confirmation change (they confirm inline through the guarded read-back and never enter the twin's confirm path).
